clips.text_zh: BTC 靜咗幾星期 然後一夜爆15% 又話想上車🙄 仆街 真係每次都係咁 早兩日都唔睇 升完先黎問點入 好啦 CFD又手多多開咗一張 short 😇🙏 又係學費
clips.text_en_b1: Why does everyone want to buy BTC after the move already happened? You watch BTC do nothing for weeks and ignore it completely. Then it pumps 15% and suddenly everyone wants in. Classic late-FOMO behavior — by the time retail wakes up, the smart money already took profit on the move.
clips.source_hint: /biz/ post ranting about chasing BTC after the pump

signal.rationale: OP is implicitly calling late buyers dumb; anon framed a CFD short against the FOMO chase

clips.text_en_b2: Honestly, BTC sat there doing absolutely nothing for weeks and I completely wrote it off. Then out of nowhere it rips 15% overnight, and suddenly every retail trader under the sun wants a piece of the action. Classic late-FOMO behaviour — by the time the herd catches on, the smart money has already cashed out. I even opened a cheeky CFD short, which will probably end up being another expensive lesson in market timing.
clips.text_en_c1: It is genuinely baffling how reliably retail capitulates to FOMO precisely when the move has already been made. BTC consolidates sideways for what feels like an eternity, drawing absolutely no attention from the average punter, and then in a single overnight session it rips fifteen percent higher. Suddenly every Tom, Dick and Harry is scrambling to position long, convinced they have missed the boat. By the time the latecomers arrive, the smart money has long since distributed into that demand. Predictably, yours truly could not resist opening a CFD short on the subsequent push — call it tuition paid in full for failing to internalise the lesson.
clips.text_en_c2: The phenomenon of retail FOMO manifesting only after a substantial rally remains one of the more predictable ironies of crypto markets. Bitcoin idles, largely unremarked, for weeks on end; sentiment sags, the chart flatlines, and nobody bothers allocating capital. Then, almost overnight, a fifteen-percent vertical move occurs, and suddenly every dormant account reawakens demanding entry at exactly the worst possible juncture. By the time the average punit scrambles for exposure, the sophisticated participants — those who accumulated during the preceding apathy — have already distributed into that very enthusiasm. The reflexive human tendency to require confirmation before committing capital guarantees consistent underperformance. Personally, I capitulated, opening a CFD short almost reflexively, since the gravitational pull of contrarian positioning, however poorly timed, proved psychologically irresistible.

clips.text_en_b1: I have 9,150 DOGE. Should I try to build up to 25,000 in case it actually hits £1? I want to buy a Toyota AE86 with it. Currently sitting at 9,150 coins, target is roughly 25,000 which would be enough for a clean AE86 if the dream comes true.

signal.rationale: Anon's accumulation target is 25k DOGE to fund an AE86; long bias with multi-month horizon

clips.text_en_b2: I'm currently sitting on roughly 9,150 DOGE and wondering whether I should top it up to around 25,000 coins, just in case it somehow pulls off a run to £1. If that dream ever materialised, the profits would more or less cover a tidy Toyota AE86. Realistically though, a £1 target is pure fantasy, so I'm treating any further accumulation as tuition money while Elon keeps moving the markets.
clips.text_en_c1: I am currently holding 9,150 DOGE and entertaining the rather fanciful notion of averaging down until I accumulate roughly 25,000 coins, predicated on the hilariously improbable scenario in which the asset revisits the pound parity that early adopters briefly tasted. Should that dream materialise, the proceeds would, in theory, be sufficient to secure a clean Toyota AE86 — the vehicular holy grail for anyone who came of age watching Initial D. Realistically, the target is pure wishful thinking, but riding Musk's media appearances as a proxy catalyst keeps things entertaining enough to justify the position. Tomorrow's early shift looms regardless.
clips.text_en_c2: I currently hold approximately 9,150 DOGE, a position accumulated gradually through various small purchases during the coin's prolonged dormancy. My rather quixotic objective involves accumulating somewhere in the vicinity of 25,000 coins, predicated on the admittedly fantastical assumption that the token achieves parity with the pound sterling. Should such an improbable convergence materialise, I intend to liquidate the entirety of the position and acquire a clean Toyota AE86 — that quintessentially aspirational machine of initial-D mythology, whose values have appreciated almost as absurdly as the cryptocurrencies financing their acquisition. The probability of DOGE attaining £1 remains, by any rational metric, vanishingly remote; nevertheless, one persists in such calculations because the alternative — confronting the genuine mathematics of one's trading decisions — is considerably less diverting than entertaining grandiose automotive fantasies funded by meme-driven speculation.

clips.text_zh: Debian俾印度人接咗 一接咗就開始 vibecoding成個OS lol 咁穩定distro邊個做緊 唔係Mageia就OpenMandriva啦？ 同我公司份工一樣 AI真係乜都嚟緊 🧐
clips.text_en_b1: An Indian took over the Debian project. Immediately they began vibecoding the entire operating system, which is now being labeled Indian AI slop on /g/. People are asking what the stable distro of the future is — Mageia, OpenMandriva, or something else entirely. Phoronix covered the vote on responsible AI use.
clips.text_en_b2: Apparently an Indian contributor has taken the reins at Debian and immediately started vibecoding chunks of the operating system, which /g/ is now gleefully labelling as Indian AI slop. The whole saga has people asking what the next genuinely stable distro will actually be, whether that ends up being Mageia, OpenMandriva, or something else entirely. Phoronix ran a piece on the vote around responsible AI use, and it echoes what I keep seeing at my own job.
clips.text_en_c1: It appears Debian has effectively fallen under new stewardship, and the immediate consequence has been an aggressive push toward what can only be described as vibecoding the entire operating system. The reception has been predictably scathing, with /g/ branding the output as little more than Indian AI slop, which raises legitimate questions about where one ought to migrate if stability remains the priority. Mageia and OpenMandriva have been floated as plausible contenders, though neither carries Debian's institutional weight. Phoronix covered the underlying vote on responsible AI deployment, and frankly the parallels with my own day job are rather uncomfortably close.
clips.text_en_c2: The recent developments surrounding the Debian project have elicited considerable consternation across technical communities, particularly following assertions that the distribution's stewardship has effectively transferred to individuals whose engineering philosophy prioritises expedient, AI-assisted generation over considered systems architecture. The notion of 'vibecoding' an entire operating system — that is, delegating substantive implementation decisions to stochastic language models — represents a rather alarming inflection point for a distribution historically synonymous with conservatism, rigour, and an almost pathological devotion to stability. Predictably, the discourse has migrated toward alternative candidates: Mageia, OpenMandriva, and various Arch derivatives have all been mooted as plausible refuges for users unwilling to entrust their infrastructure to generative experimentation.

clips.text_zh: 有人話 講一句「亞洲男人平均矮啲」 然後叫人接average 識接就正常 唔識就 IQ低 🧐 真係4chan式IQ test 我同事Tommy都係咁 一講統計就膠膠噏 仲有六壬堂sifu都話今年唔好亂郁
clips.text_en_b1: Someone on /pol/ claims the fastest IQ test is making a generalized statement about a group, like "Asian men are shorter on average." If they reply with "not all Asian men are short" or "I know a tall Asian guy," you are dealing with a genuinely low-IQ person who cannot understand statistical averages.
clips.text_en_b2: Someone on /pol/ insists the fastest IQ test around is dropping a generalisation like "Asian men are shorter on average" and watching how people respond. Anyone who jumps in with "not all Asian men are short" or trots out their one tall Asian friend is essentially confirming they can't grasp basic statistical averages. It's a depressingly reliable filter, and frankly my colleague Tommy falls for the exact same trap every single time.
clips.text_en_c1: A particularly cynical heuristic circulating on /pol/ posits that the most efficient IQ test available consists simply of stating a statistical generality — something to the effect of Asian men being, on average, shorter than their Western counterparts. Should the respondent immediately counter with anecdotal evidence such as 'well, my friend is quite tall,' or insist that the average does not apply to every individual, one can confidently conclude that one is dealing with someone who fundamentally cannot conceptualise what an average actually means. My colleague Tommy exhibits precisely this tendency whenever statistical reasoning enters the conversation, degenerating into incoherent bluster within seconds.
clips.text_en_c2: A remarkably reductive intelligence heuristic has been circulating, ostensibly formulated by individuals who have confused contrarianism for insight. The proposition runs thus: proffer a statistically defensible generalisation — for instance, the empirically verifiable observation that Asian men exhibit, on aggregate, marginally lower mean stature than certain other demographic cohorts — and thereafter evaluate the respondent's reaction. Should they immediately retreat into anecdotal exceptions ('not all Asian men are short,' 'my friend is quite tall'), one may reasonably conclude that their cognitive apparatus cannot accommodate distributional thinking; that they persistently conflate individual instances with population-level parameters. The test, while admittedly glib, exposes a genuine epistemological deficiency. An inability to distinguish between a statement concerning central tendency and one asserting universal applicability suggests either inadequate statistical literacy or a more profound reluctance to engage with abstract reasoning.

clips.text_zh: 2012年 LoL budget 30M 120個developer 2026年 2 BILLION 6000個developer 我睇緊S15都覺得個game越嚟越膠 咁多錢做出嚟係咁 多餘晒 lol btw考牌書睇到第三chapter 真係靠AI續命
clips.text_en_b1: Look at the difference between League of Legends in 2012 and 2026. In 2012 the budget was 30 million dollars with about 120 developers. By 2026 the budget is 2 billion dollars and the team is around 6,000 developers. Same franchise, completely different scale, and honestly the game feels worse for it.
clips.source_hint: /v/ thread on LoL dev cost inflation
clips.text_en_b2: Take a look at how dramatically League of Legends has scaled over the years. Back in 2012 the budget sat at around 30 million dollars with a team of roughly 120 developers, whereas by 2026 Riot is pouring in roughly 2 billion dollars and employing close to 6,000 people. Same franchise, vastly different scope, and yet watching the current season the gameplay honestly feels worse rather than better, which is hard to swallow.
clips.text_en_c1: The trajectory of League of Legends' development budget over the intervening decade and change is nothing short of staggering when laid out in raw numbers. Back in 2012 the operation ran on a comparatively modest thirty million dollars with a team of approximately 120 developers; by 2026 that figure has ballooned to a scarcely believable two billion dollars, with the headcount expanding to roughly 6,000. Despite this extraordinary forty-fold increase in resources, watching the current season one cannot shake the suspicion that the end product has somehow deteriorated. Diminishing returns appear to have set in with a vengeance, leaving one to wonder where precisely the money has gone.
clips.text_en_c2: The financial trajectory of League of Legends across a fourteen-year interval furnishes a compelling, if dispiriting, case study in the diminishing returns characteristic of escalating production budgets. In 2012, the title operated on a comparatively modest thirty-million-dollar budget, sustained by approximately 120 developers — a configuration that nevertheless produced what remains, for many, the genre's definitive iteration. Contrast this with the contemporary situation: a development apparatus numbering roughly 6,000 personnel, consuming something approaching two billion dollars annually, yet delivering a product that, by widespread critical consensus, has palpably deteriorated. The paradox is unmistakable: exponential resource expansion has coincided with a measurable decline in both mechanical coherence and artistic vision. Whether one attributes this to bureaucratic bloat, design-committee timidity, or the perpetual scope-creep endemic to live-service architecture, the outcome remains identical — the player receives less.

clips.text_zh: Cut 3個月瘦45磅 但肌肉同力量都走晒 gym真係打到仆街 心口做set好似要死咁 又食唔落嘢 要強制自己食 睇完即刻whatsapp肥仔信 問佢聽日一唔一齊打spar lol🙏
clips.text_en_b1: How are you supposed to lift heavy and get enough protein on a cut? I lost 45 pounds in 3 months but I definitely lost muscle and strength. The gym absolutely kills me — I can't go hard because my body won't let me, squats make my heart feel like it's giving out, and I can barely eat more than a couple of times a…
clips.source_hint: /fit/ thread on losing strength while cutting
clips.text_en_b2: I've been running a cut for about three months and dropped roughly 45 pounds, but along with the fat I've noticeably lost both muscle and strength, which is incredibly frustrating. The gym absolutely wipes me out — even a single working set on chest feels borderline dangerous, my heart rate goes through the roof, and forcing myself to eat enough protein throughout the day has become a genuine struggle.
clips.text_en_c1: Maintaining any semblance of productive hypertrophy on an aggressive cut is, frankly, an exercise in masochism that I would not wish upon anyone. Over the past three months I have shed a not inconsiderable forty-five pounds, yet the accompanying erosion of both muscle mass and strength has been substantial enough that each session now feels like an act of self-harm. Compound movements in particular have become genuinely punishing — pressing weight on the chest feels akin to courting cardiac arrest, while appetite suppression renders adequate caloric intake a constant battle of willpower against one's own physiology.
clips.text_en_c2: The physiological contradictions inherent to aggressive caloric restriction while attempting to preserve lean tissue constitute one of bodybuilding's more punishing paradoxes. My recent experience illustrates the predicament with uncomfortable clarity: over a three-month span, I shed approximately forty-five pounds, yet the composition of that loss proved devastatingly unfavourable. Strength metrics have cratered, muscle cross-sections have visibly diminished, and the gym — once a locus of competence and progressive overload — has become a venue for protracted suffering. Compound movements, particularly heavy squats, induce cardiac responses suggesting imminent cardiovascular compromise. Appetite, meanwhile, has evaporated entirely; meals require deliberate, almost ceremonial enforcement, since the body's homeostatic mechanisms interpret the deficit as approaching famine. The entire enterprise feels less like physique optimisation and considerably more like managed deterioration.

clips.text_zh: 有人問點解得一套anime ending做到 plot全部收晒 又冇爛尾 到底係行業問題定寫劇本問題 我諗咗一陣 可能Gundam 00算一個？ Demon Slayer就麻麻 總之要做工程就最忌爛尾 考牌都唔例外 lol
clips.text_en_b1: Years later and this is probably still the best anime ending I have ever seen. Why are there barely any other anime that tie up all of their plot points and loose ends in such a satisfying way? Is it an industry problem or a writing problem? Most modern endings feel rushed compared to the classics.
clips.source_hint: /a/ thread praising a perfect anime ending
clips.text_en_b2: Even years later, this is arguably still the most satisfying anime ending I've ever come across, because it manages to wrap up virtually every plot thread without leaving anything dangling. That raises a broader question: why do so few modern series manage the same feat? Whether you blame shifting industry priorities or simply weaker writing, most contemporary finales feel rushed and hollow compared to the classics, and the gap shows.
clips.text_en_c1: The persistent scarcity of anime conclusions that manage to deliver genuine narrative closure without resorting to the customary rushed, inconclusive denouement remains something of an industry enigma. Whether one attributes this recurring failure to structural commercial pressures, broadcast slot constraints, or simply a dearth of writers capable of architecting satisfactory resolutions is largely a matter of speculation, though the latter explanation strikes me as more plausible. Gundam 00 stands as a comparatively rare exemplar of the form, whereas modern offerings such as Demon Slayer demonstrate precisely the hasty, unsatisfying wrap-up that has become endemic to the medium.
clips.text_en_c2: The perpetual discourse surrounding anime conclusions invariably circles back to a rather dispiriting observation: genuinely satisfying narrative resolutions have become increasingly anomalous within the medium. One seeks works that honour their accumulated threads — that eschew the convenience of abrupt terminations, the narrative cowardice of sequel-baiting, and the particular disappointment of deflations where intricate machinations resolve into mere petering-out. The contemporary landscape offers few exemplars; Demon Slayer, despite its commercial dominance, rather exemplifies the problem through its compressed and emotionally perfunctory conclusion. Gundam 00, perhaps, approaches the threshold of adequate resolution, though even there one senses compromises demanded by commercial considerations. The underlying pathology likely transcends individual writers: structural incentives reward perpetuation over conclusion, since ongoing franchises generate revenue that concluded ones cannot.
